attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his authored newsletter post. 'They' refers to companies and executives. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: The unhedged 'will' makes this a firm forecast that companies will replace workers they think can be automated. The normalisation keeps the 'believe can be automated' condition. 'Gladly' and 'in a heartbeat' are rhetorical descriptions of readiness, not measurable terms.

contract.note: The plain reading (several employers complete AI substitutions, including creative or editorial work) is an ordinary reading. It treats the named occupations as examples, not separate tests. It is mildly lenient on 'any other role', but reasonable for a claim about how companies are disposed to act.

evidence.note: Ars Technica, dated after the post. G/O Media fired the Gizmodo en Español editorial staff on 2023-08-29 and switched the site to AI translation. A dismissed writer is named. This is a completed editorial substitution.

Duolingo CEO on the Q4 2023 earnings call (a company disclosure). He confirms translation and content contractors were cut, with AI 'probably' the biggest reason. This is a second completed AI-linked substitution and an admission against the company's interest.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met. Two companies completed AI-linked substitutions of editorial or translation workers after 2023-08-03: Gizmodo en Español in Aug 2023 and Duolingo, confirmed Feb 2024. The packet contains no counterevidence. Caveats: the evidence shows no replacement of artists specifically and does not measure how widespread this is, and Duolingo's attribution to AI is lightly hedged. Under the fair plain reading, the claim is supported.
